young.html: Adam Smith was a Scottish professor who wanted to know: what makes a country rich? Not gold piled up in a king's treasury, he said, but all the useful things its people make and trade.

He started with something tiny: a pin. One worker alone, making pins from start to finish, could hardly make one pin a day, and certainly not twenty. But in a pin factory Smith visited, ten workers each did one or two steps, cutting wire, sharpening points, putting on heads, and together they made about 48,000 pins a day!

Smith called this the division of labor. When people specialize and then trade, everyone can have more. The baker bakes, the butcher cuts meat, and they trade, each helping the other while helping themselves.

full.html: Adam Smith (1723–1790) taught moral philosophy at Glasgow and first became known for The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), a book about sympathy and conscience. An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations appeared in 1776, the year of the American Declaration of Independence. It argues against mercantilism, the policy of piling up gold and silver through trade surpluses, protecting home industries and granting monopolies.

full.title: Smith's pin numbers
full.q: Ten workers make about twelve pounds of pins a day, with upwards of 4,000 pins in a pound. How many pins is that per worker?
steps: $12 \times 4000 = 48{,}000$ pins a day for the ten.
Working alone, Smith says, each could certainly not make twenty: $4800 \div 20 = 240$, so at least 240 times as many.
full.a: 4,800 pins each, about 240 times what one could make alone

full.html: Smith gives three reasons the division of labor raises output: greater skill from doing one task, time saved in not switching tasks, and the invention of machines by workers focused on one job. And it is limited by the extent of the market: a village can't support a full-time pin-maker, a great trading city can.

full.text: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest. We address ourselves, not to their humanity, but to their self-love, and never talk to them of our own necessities, but of their advantages.

full.html: People have, Smith says, a natural "propensity to truck, barter, and exchange." Prices tend toward a natural price that covers wages, profit and rent, though the market price rises and falls with supply and demand. In Book IV he says that a merchant who seeks only his own gain is often "led by an invisible hand to promote an end which was no part of his intention": the good of society. The phrase appears only once in the book.

full.text: The system of natural liberty, and its limits

full.html: Smith favors a "system of natural liberty" in which each person may pursue his own interest within the laws of justice. But he assigns the government real duties: defense, the administration of justice, and public works and institutions that private profit wouldn't provide, including roads, harbors and schooling for the common people. He warns that merchants and manufacturers often conspire to raise prices and seek monopolies from government, and that the repetitive work of the division of labor can dull workers' minds unless education counters it.

Thinking Smith said greed is good or that government should do nothing. He wrote a whole book on sympathy and virtue, and he gave government important tasks; he thought free exchange within just laws served the public better than monopolies and trade restrictions.

deep.html: The Wealth of Nations is often called the founding book of modern economics. British trade policy moved toward freer trade in the 19th century, partly under its influence. Later economists kept Smith's questions but changed many answers: his theory of value, which gave labor a central place, was developed by Ricardo and then by Marx (in the next era) in a direction Smith did not take, while later economists explained prices by supply and demand at the margin.

Economists today still argue about how far markets should be left free and where government should step in, for public goods, monopolies, or helping those left behind. Both sides often claim Smith, and his own mixed view is a reason to read him directly.
